comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C48-C53 regarding testable predictions from the computational model. Both evaluations find these predictions SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes they are internally consistent and logically follow from model structure, while peer reviewers emphasize they are 'intriguing and testable' with compelling modeling data.

Perfect agreement on claims C78-C81 regarding mechanistic explanations for split-belt locomotion. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes consistency with model architecture, while peer reviewers note the systematic consideration of how model states relate to experimental data.

Perfect agreement on claims C17-C18, C59-C60 regarding reconciliation of historical theories. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes it as a unified framework, while peer reviewers call it 'a major benefit' that bridges various CPG concepts and resolves contradictions.

Perfect agreement on claims C64, C66 regarding clinical implications and predictions. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes logical extension requiring human validation, while peer reviewers emphasize the testable and transformative nature of these insights.

Strong agreement on claims C73-C77 regarding model's quantitative reproduction of experimental data. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes qualitative and quantitative agreement validating core mechanisms, while peer reviewers note the model was 'closely tuned to match a huge range of experimental data' with high plausibility.

Strong agreement on claims C35-C37, C39-C40 regarding sensory feedback mechanisms. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes consistency with known physiological mechanisms, while peer reviewers explicitly praise the biological grounding and note sensory feedback's crucial role at lower speeds.

Strong agreement on claims C2, C45-C47 regarding the model's core contribution of three-state behavior. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes successful reproduction of experimental observations, while peer reviewers call it 'a truly major advance' with 'transformative effect' on the field.

Agreement on claims C19-C22 regarding experimental observations from Figure 1. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate sample sizes and statistical measures, while peer reviewers accept these experimental observations without challenge as part of the strong experimental foundation.

Agreement on claims C23-C26 regarding split-belt locomotion experimental data. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistent patterns with appropriate controls, while peer reviewers highlight the inclusion of split-belt treadmill data as a strength.

Agreement on claims C54-C55 regarding testable predictions about slow gait. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval describes it as a plausible explanation for experimental observations, while peer reviewers call it 'another important step forward' regarding neural control of slow gait.

Agreement on claims C32-C34 regarding model features based on spinal circuitry. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistency with known organization, while peer reviewers explicitly praise the biological detail including commissural interneurons and other interneuron types.

Divergent evaluations on claims C61-C62 regarding behavioral implications. OpenEval rates these UNCERTAIN due to speculation about behavioral contexts not directly tested, while peer reviewers find them SUPPORTED, calling them 'intriguing and testable predictions' and 'important step forward.'

Partial agreement on model architecture claims. OpenEval R3 covers C14-C15, C27-C28, C56-C57 (all SUPPORTED), while peer R10 covers C27-C28, C14, C32-C34 (all SUPPORTED). Both affirm the model's biological grounding and ability to reproduce experimental observations.

Partial agreement on claims C56-C57 regarding multi-state conceptual framework. Both evaluations find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes mechanistic explanations for regime transitions, while peer reviewers praise moving away from classical half-center concepts and bridging various CPG concepts.

Partial overlap on claim C6 regarding spinal injury implications. OpenEval rates C6, C61-C62 as UNCERTAIN due to speculation, while peer reviewers find C5-C6 SUPPORTED, noting the model shows spinal injury is 'stuck' in low-speed state-machine behavior as an important finding.

Partial overlap on claims C41-C42 regarding model features. OpenEval R7 covers C16, C41-C43 (SUPPORTED) emphasizing mechanistic explanation for intact vs spinal differences, while peer R6 covers C35-C37, C39-C40, C41-C42 (SUPPORTED) focusing on sensory feedback implementation.

Minimal overlap on claim C72 regarding overall model performance. Both evaluations find this SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes it's a summary statement supported by detailed comparisons, while peer reviewers affirm the model's ability to reproduce experimental data with high plausibility.

Minimal overlap on claim C15 regarding model architecture. Both evaluations find this SUPPORTED. OpenEval groups it with broader model architecture claims, while peer reviewers include it with the three-state behavior as a major advance.
